Have you ever heard that old tale of David and Goliath?

Rock slings really can kill a man, and you'll realize this is truth as soon as you successfully fling your first sizable stone.

... You will however find that there is something left to be desired in accuracy. Learning to sling a rock takes a bit of practice on it's own, but developing deadly aim is something that can take years.

But don't be discouraged from learning to use this amazing ancient weapon:

  1. They are very simple to make
  2. There is no need to bring heavy ammunition with you while on a hike, since you can quickly collect a pouch-full of stones once you near the hunting grounds
  3. The sling itself is very light-weight, and can be wrapped upon itself for convenient, compact storage
  4. There's nothing quite like the feeling of sending a rock flying at incredible speeds with very little effort, and having it harangue it's way into the target with a crack!

The best source I've found to learn about all the various types of slings, along with their construction is Slinging.org

I encourage anyone interested in survival, or who wants to teach their child a great way to "hunt" squirrels and rabbits to pick this skill up.

I agree! Especially living in the pacific northwest where dense foliage can make for difficult small game hunting, a along shot is an affordable way to go!

Personally I use a wrist rocket and not the traditional method, although I have had experience making and using them.

The skill required to get a kill shot with a sling-shot vs a rock sling are worlds apart. You can get good in a week with a sling-shot, it can take months (years from most accounts) with a rock sling.

That said, with a larger rock sling, you can fling river stones which are like... 4x8x4 inches (rounded of course), kinda like a large potato. That hits you at full speed, you're likely to lose whatever it hits.
